subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
This is the one section of the bill that has been of considerable concern to members from the province of British Columbia. The calibre of debate has been sufficiently high on this subject that I am not going to say anything that will lower it. The people of British Columbia do not want any amendment made in the bill at the expense of any other part of Canada. We have not built up what we have in that province today by enforcing harsher conditions on any other part of Canada, and we do not intend to do so in the future. However, what we are particularly concerned about in this section is that the transcontinental rates are the ones upon which is to be founded the entire intention of the section and the most important part of it, namely that in the intermediate territory the rate that shall apply from the eastern territory to the western territory or from the western territory to the eastern territory shall not be greater to any point than one and one-third the competitive transcontinental rate.
Our excellent friends from Alberta are delighted with this legislation, and I can understand their delight when for many years they have been paying rates which were sometimes two and a half to three times the transcontinental rate. To have relief proffered in the form of an over-all rate to all intermediate points not greater than one and one-third the transcontinental rate is a most engaging prospect. However, I should like to draw their attention to this point, and I should like the minister to make some comment concerning it. Members from Alberta must remember that the one and one-third rate is dependent entirely upon the maintenance of the transcontinental competitive rate. We and the representatives employed by the

Railway Act
province of British Columbia to appear before the committee were of the opinion at one time that we could include something in the section which would ensure that the transcontinental competitive rates would apply, but we are told that by the very nature of competitive rates such an amendment cannot be included.
Therefore we are concerned with this section which endeavours to spell out the meaning of the national policy to bring relief to a great part of the prairie provinces, because in order to bring that relief we must have maintenance of the transcontinental rates. If I may revert to section 332A, we were inclined to believe that there was adequate provision under subsection 3 of that section, which reads as follows:
The board may disallow any tariff or any portion thereof that it considers to be contrary to the national freight rates policy, and may require the company, within a prescribed time, to substitute a tariff satisfactory to the board in lieu thereof, or may prescribe other tolls in lieu of the tolls so disallowed.
We thought that was ample provision. Many people who gave evidence-and this was also indicated in many briefs sent to us-indicated that they thought the freight rate structure could suffer if it were made too rigid, that after all the board of transport commissioners had to make decisions in these matters and that as much leeway as possible should be given to them. I suggest that subsection 3 of section 332A gives all the leeway in the world to the board of transport commissioners to provide a satisfactory rate in any direction for any commodity. But in order to pinpoint national policy as it may affect the prairie provinces it is proposed to include this one and one-third provision based upon the transcontinental rate. It comes to us repeatedly that relief for the prairie provinces is founded completely upon maintenance of the transcontinental rates.
We had some evidence on the part of the railways to this effect: Well, if you do not have the transcontinental rates we will put in a low commodity rate that will not hurt you too much. That evidence is to be found on page 211 of the proceedings of the committee. The witness, Mr. Knowles, suggested that such a low commodity rate would not be too high either. Our only point is that we are interested in the maintenance of the transcontinental rates. We want to point out that the relief for the prairie provinces which is proffered in the substance and the spirit of this bill is dependent upon the maintenance of the transcontinental rates, and we are further advised that we cannot include an amendment to maintain those rates. That is
[Mr. Laing.l
why we took the stand we did in the committee, and I would much prefer to see 332B dropped entirely.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
It must be evident by now that there is a weakness in section 33 2B, which deals with the transcontinental rates and the imposition thereon of what we have been calling the one and one-third rule. When you look back over the meetings of the special committee, and when you look at the debate in this committee so far in connection with this bill, it is a strange thing that most of the sections have gone through, both in the special committee and here, without any great delay; but when you come to section 332B you find a very sharp difference of opinion, and that difference of opinion is absolutely non-partisan. In view of the nature of our country it happens to be sectional.
What is wrong with section 332B that it has aroused this difference of opinion? I submit for the attention of the committee that section 332B, based as it is on a recommendation of the royal commission, has not back of it the same weight of opinion that we find with regard to other recommendations of the royal commission. We have been told of the number of meetings that the royal commission had, and of the opportunities afforded all interested parties to make representations. Over a period of a year and a half the royal commission investigated all these problems; and it is only reasonable to expect that when there has been complete investigation, when every party interested has made his statement, a finding of a royal commission should receive due consideration. I think that with respect to other parts of this particular bill due weight has been given to the recommendations of the royal commission. But here, in so far as I can discover, and based on the statements made by the official representatives of the province of Manitoba and of the city of Winnipeg who appeared before the special committee, this particular finding of the royal commission did not have back of it the complete evidence that is back of other findings. Just let me read what counsel for the province of Manitoba said when he appeared before the special committee:
The recommendation of the Turgeon royal commission (p. 100 of the report) on which the section is presumably based, was not advocated by any person or organization appearing before the commission. The railways did not suggest it as sound from a rate-making point of view. The provinces and other interested groups did not suggest it as sound from either a rate-making or economic point of view. In short, the suggested 1} rule is entirely arbitrary in character, unsupported by any representation before the Turgeon commission.

In other words, had Manitoba then been aware that this one and one-third rule was going to be a finding of the commission, that province would have made a detailed study of the matter and would have made an effective presentation. I presume that British Columbia would have done the same thing, and the other provinces entering into it. Then what would we have had? We would have had a deliberate study on the part of the royal commission of the effects of that particular rule, and then a finding; and based on that finding, legislation. Had that happened, we would not have been in the same position in the special committee nor here in the committee of the whole. We might have raised an objection, whatever the finding would have been, but naturally the objections would not carry as much weight as I suggest the objections that have been put forward so far do carry.
I have put before the committee of the whole for its consideration the point of view of the province of Manitoba, the city of Winnipeg and the Winnipeg chamber of commerce. This point of view is a serious and considered one. The people who presented the briefs to our special committee were men who have been concerned with and engaged for a long time in the study of freight rates. They had competent economic advisers and men who were able to give them adequate advice on the freight rates problem, and I think their point of view deserves very careful consideration. In fact I thought that at the meeting of our special committee the point of view against 332B in its present form was rather completely set forth, and I entertained the hope at the time that some modifications would be introduced, just as in other aspects of the bill we have had certain modifications brought in. However, that did not happen, so we have reached this stage where it is necessary to put the position of Manitoba before the committee of the whole so the committee will have a full understanding of our objection to this section.
As the brief for Manitoba represented, Manitoba states that a violation of the general principles of the bill has occurred. This bill is aimed generally at equalization, and this method of dealing with the transcontinental rate involves something that is not equalization. At the bottom of page 125 of the report the royal commission points out that equalization is not going to be obtained very quickly; that is, some study must be made of the problem, and the report says:
Undoubtedly many serious problems are involved, for example the effect that the proposals may have on railway revenues, on established industries and on trade and market patterns. All of these things
Railway Act
are matters of the utmost importance. Having regard to the large number of rate changes which will be involved, the problem is one peculiarly for the board to resolve finally after the general freight rate investigation and after all parties who may be affected by the proposals have had an opportunity of being heard.
Well, no one can find fault with that suggestion in the report. Surely it is a reasonable and sane way to put into effect any alteration in the freight rate structure. If that were done in connection with this particular proposal in 332B, the position of Manitoba and the city of Winnipeg would be that there could be no objection. If the board were empowered, before putting it into operation, to investigate its effect, if any, on established industries and on trade and market patterns, we could scarcely raise objection, but there seems to be no opportunity for doing that. It is going to be written into the statute and may be applied immediately, and in our opinion Manitoba will not benefit thereby; or at least, if there is some benefit thereby, Manitoba's competitive position will be endangered to some extent.
Just to summarize the point of view of the Manitoba government let me read just one paragraph from the brief presented before the special committee:
We think that section 332B is wrong both in principle and in practice, because it would give to a restricted area a special low rate which is hot justified by the competitive tests of section 331 or by the national freight rates policy of equalization as set out in section 332A.
The effect would inevitably be to reduce railway revenue in that area below the level which is reasonable and proper under an equalized rate structure, with the result that other areas would be called upon to pay slightly higher rates to make up the necessary revenue.
Then on the next page there are two sentences I should like to quote:
The disturbance of existing and long-established competitive positions of businesses in the various centres of western Canada.
This would result from the application of this rule.
The distortion of a sound set of principles laid down in sections 329, 331 and 332A by the special concession to a particular area on a particular type of traffic as set out in 332B.
The city of Winnipeg presented a similar point of view. It all comes down to this. We are of the opinion that there will be an adverse effect on Manitoba's industrial development, particularly in respect of steel products. We in Manitoba sometimes feel that people are not aware of the extent of the industrialization of the province. My argument is based on the effect of section 332B of the Railway Act on our industrialization.

Railway Act
Without enlarging upon it to the fullest extent, I want to say a word about Manitoba's industrial development. It has been proceeding at a very satisfactory rate during the last few years. We take a considerable interest and pride in that fact. Anyone who is interested in getting a more complete picture may refer to the Toronto Saturday Night of November 24, 1951. On page 23 there is a useful article by Mr. Carlyle Allison concerning Manitoba's industrial development, and the introductory sentence is in rather forceful language. It reads:
It is a sore point in Manitoba that eastern Canada-and particularly Ottawa-still regards the keystone province as primarily agricultural . . .
Manitoba has a thoroughly developed agricultural economy which has been the backbone of the province for a great many years. At the same time we are developing an industrial side, the extent of which can be seen in this article. The whole point of my argument is that when you have an industrial development the freight rate structure becomes just as important to that section of your economy as the freight rate structure is to the movement of your agricultural products.
I quote again from this article in Saturday Night:
The total value of all farm production in Manitoba in 1950 was $298,952,000; the gross value of manufactured goods produced in Manitoba in 1950 was estimated at $525 million.
Just to complete the industrial picture, since the beginning of world war II the number of manufacturing firms grew from 1,000 to more than 1,600, and their employees from 24,000 to 43,000. In 1951 alone 25 per cent of die province's manufacturers extended their plant facilities. It is because of the development of Manitoba's industry that we are so concerned about any alteration in the freight rate structure which may adversely affect that industry. Our industry is not located solely in the city of Winnipeg and suburbs. Brandon, Portage and other places in Manitoba are gradually taking part in this industrial development and will similarly be affected.
As I said, steel seems to be the product which is most likely to be affected by this rule in section 332B. By checking through the Winnipeg telephone directory I found that there were twenty-four firms advertising themselves as producers or fabricators of iron or steel. In the Canada Year Book I discovered that 10,000 people are employed in industries that have to do with iron and steel. Many of these people are employed in the railway shops, but through correspondence with Winnipeg I have

discovered that there are certainly 5,000 employees who are directly employed in these various industries I have mentioned. A new plant for the fabrication of steel has just been erected at a cost of half a million dollars. I have mentioned that steel fabrication is an important part of Manitoba's industrial production, and if her competitive position in that field is endangered, as is suggested by this brief, our hope is that some attention will be paid to the matter and our position restored, or else assurance given that the board of transport commissioners will go slowly in making any change which will adversely affect our industry.
It is an interesting investigation to consider the interrelation of the economy of the western provinces and the trade that flows between these provinces. It is not to our advantage if any of the western provinces are weakened in any way. It is not to the advantage of any of the other western provinces if Manitoba is weakened in any way. As I mentioned yesterday I am sympathetic towards the point of view of the province of Alberta, and I hope that province will be sympathetic towards the point of view of Manitoba. With the development of Manitoba and the subsequent increase of population, there will be a market for Alberta products. We have not the advantages of coal or oil, and consequently each year we import from Alberta 600,000 tons of coal and an estimated 6 million barrels of oil. It is a large and growing interprovincial commerce, and the maintenance of Manitoba's industries means the development of Manitoba's population and the consequent greater dependence upon the provinces of the west.
In conclusion I suggest that the proposal put forward in the brief of the city of Winnipeg is the one that should be considered. After all it is a reasonable suggestion, and does not ask for anything more than fair treatment. I read from the brief:
We respectfully suggest that ... if the mandatory language of section 332B be modified to permit the board some discretion which would enable it to relate the intermediate rate to the normal rate as circumstances may warrant, most of our apprehension would be alleviated.
I think that is a fair and reasonable presentation of the point of view of Manitoba, and that it should be given serious consideration here. What purpose will we have achieved if the board of transport commissioners is going to be faced, year after year, with a conflict over something which is now rather hastily written into the act? Surely the opposition that has been developed to section 332B is an indication of conflict in the future unless there is some modification of that particular

section. Modification could surely be made with a view to recognizing the established positions of the provinces concerned.

I have risen to speak only briefly because I must say that this question of the mechanics of freight rates is to me a bit of an enigma, and I am not given to speaking on subjects about which I know little. I know the attitude of some of the people of British Columbia towards this section of this bill, and I rise particularly for the purpose of supporting the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver South. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just taken his seat feels, perhaps as much as I do, that the eastern portion of British Columbia may either be adversely affected by this legislation or be benefited. As a British Columbian I rise to take exception to this clause because I feel that it adversely affects the province of British Columbia. Many of my views have already been expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
Railway Act
However, some evidence was submitted to the committee which I feel should at this time go into the record.
Section 332A deals exclusively with the question of transcontinental competitive rates. Our understanding of transcontinental competitive rates is that they may be continued only so long as the board of transport commissioners is assured that the railway companies are making a profit, or at least that they are compensatory, and that all commodities hauled at those rates will bring some measure of return to the railways.
Before going further I think it would be well to remind the committee that British Columbia, which contains a fairly large population, is certainly the province that is the greatest distance from the industrial central portion of Canada, and that with commodity and mileage rates we pay an amount greater than that paid by any other province, according to the distance from the central area. That is, if we are 700 miles farther west, we pay that much more on our commodity and) mileage rates. We therefore are at a grave disadvantage in this respect. If the transcontinental rates are to be maintained they must be compensatory, as I have said previously. If the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan have been plundered-and some of the members from Alberta have seemed to try to give that impression-a large amount of money must be involved. When the one and one-third rule is applied, there will be a measure of loss to the railways on the transcontinental rates. If there is a loss due to the return under the one and one-third rule, there must be an increase in the transcontinental rates. It is on that basis that we from British Columbia feel there is a grave danger of the transcontinental rates either being abolished or increased. Despite the feeling that is at present abroad in Alberta and Saskatchewan, despite the fact that they feel they are going to receive great benefits from this one and one-third rule, we feel it is quite possible that they will stand to lose as well as British Columbia.
It has been said that many of the briefs we have received are from quarters which we may say have no actual remunerative interest in the question, at least as far as the political aspect is concerned. We have a brief from the Canadian industrial traffic league. This, of course, is in the records of the committee, but I should like to read from it at this time:
Our concern is, primarily, with subsection, 2 (b) of proposed section 332B which would establish a specific maximum to intermediate points over a transcontinental competitive rate. This subsection would, in effect, decree rates by statute, although such rates are not named specifically.

Railway Act
Then further down:
We strongly recommend to the committee that further study be given to the method of dealing with this problem which has been evolved ini the United States under what is commonly known as "fourth section relief." In brief, as applied to transcontinental rates this requires that the railways make such rates applicable to intermediate points unless the interstate commerce commission grants their application to do otherwise.
If that were written into this section it would provide relief, so that if any rate were found to be non-compensatory it could be appealed to the board, and some measure of assurance could be given that the transcontinental rate would not be lost.
Then the Montreal board of trade, referring to section 332B, says:
As with other shippers, there is no opposition to any effort to provide lower rates to any intermediate points. It is felt, therefore, that the transcontinental competitive rates should have intermediate application but that should the carriers require relief from this intermediate application, then such relief should be effected by application of the carriers to the board of transport commissioners rather than by statute as this section would require.
And then the board of trade of the city of Toronto, with respect to the same section, states:
In such a situation, it is possible that the railways may have to reconsider their position respecting these rates-
That is, competitive transcontinental rates.
-and in that event it is conceivable that they may be forced to cancel the transcontinental rates and probably be compelled also to review the existing system of publishing competitive rates in the light of the possible general effects such legislation may have on these rates.
As I say, that is our fear. However, if the minister can assure us that we are not in immediate danger of losing our preferred position of being a coastal province, and if there is no danger of losing our transcontinental rates, then I am prepared to support this section of the bill.

speechtext:
I feel it is quite significant that this debate is being conducted in the very moderate terms which characterize the speeches being made. This is especially true in view of the sectional interests that seem to be involved. I think that very moderation with which members from different parts of the country are speaking indicates our desire, no matter from what part of the country we may come, to take whatever stand is in the national interest. Furthermore I think it indicates that if from the point of view of any section of the country we feel there is a particular point we have to make, or a particular position we have to put forward, none of us wants to do that to the detriment of any other section.

I believe what I have just said characterizes the remarks of several of those who have spoken just now. Naturally I am particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, since both of us come from the same area. I agree with pretty well everything be said. I think there may be some slight differences of emphasis I would wish to make, in respect of what I think should be done; but we each appear to have the same approach to the matter. I am sure the committee listened with interest to the statistics the hon. member placed before us concerning the growing industrial activities of our city of Winnipeg and our province of Manitoba. I think hon. members generally will agree that once the life of a community becomes centred around and established upon certain industries, and certain things being done, one should not see those industries disturbed unduly unless there is good cause for such disturbance or appropriate compensation.
I too think the representations made to the special committee on railway legislation by the Manitoba government and those representing the Winnipeg chamber of commerce were likewise moderate. They did, of course, express opposition to the one and one-third rule. I am not so sure I can go that far and say that I would want the one and one-third rule deleted from the bill, because I cannot get over the fact that, to me, it is in the national interest that the advantage that the one and one-third rule will give, particularly to areas such as Saskatchewan and Alberta, should be enjoyed. That is one of the aspects of the approach toward equalization which has been a goal for many years. Nevertheless I do think it is perfectly proper for the people of Winnipeg, and for those of us who represent that area, to look at the effects of that one and one-third rule in so far as it applies to the Winnipeg area.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has already referred to the brief presented to the committee by the government of Manitoba. I have it before me; and I am thinking in particular of the example given in that brief respecting freight rates on iron and steel products from Hamilton to Winnipeg, and on to Battleford. It was pointed out that the present rate from Hamilton to Winnipeg on steel products is $1.64 and from Winnipeg to Battleford $1.10, or a total of $2.74 for the entire distance if the material is shipped from Hamilton to Winnipeg and then shipped again from Winnipeg to Battleford.
The rate from Hamilton to Edmonton at the present time is $2.91. By making further reference to the Manitoba brief I would point

out that when the one and one-third rule becomes effective, since the transcontinental rate to Vancouver is only $1.48, the rate to Edmonton would be only one and one-third times that, or $1.97. That through rate from Hamilton to Edmonton would thus be less than the combined rate for iron and steel products from Hamilton to Winnipeg and from Winnipeg on to Battleford or Edmonton. As a matter of fact under this new arrangement it would be possible for iron and steel products to be shipped from Hamilton to Edmonton and back to Battleford, cheaper than they could be shipped from Hamilton to Winnipeg and then from Winnipeg to Battleford.
It is precisely that kind of anomaly, that kind of inequality, that equalization is supposed to get away from. I welcome the fact that in many instances this sort of difficulty is being ironed out. That is one of the main purposes of this legislation. But it does seem that Manitoba has made a case to the effect that some new anomalies of this kind may be created for Manitoba by the strict application of the one and one-third rule. I am not one who will ask that Winnipeg or any other part of the country be kept in a protected position. It is my view that when there is an attempt to follow that theory or philosophy the people of the country sooner or later have to pay for it in higher costs.
At the same time I think Winnipeg is perfectly justified in asking that it ought not to be placed in a disadvantageous position, and it does seem to me that something could be done to solve the kind of problem outlined in the Manitoba brief. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in my opinion approached this question in a statesmanlike fashion. If I heard him correctly, it was not suggested that we should put up a fight against the one and one-third rule but that the board of transport commissioners should consider problems of this kind and try to find some way of solving them. The hon. member referred to the request from Winnipeg that the board endeavour to relate intermediate rates to the normal rates.
What interests me even more than that are what are sometimes referred to as in-transit rates. I know this matter was discussed in the special committee only briefly, and the reference to it will be found on pages 143 and 144 of the proceedings of the committee. At that time I believe the chairman suggested that a slight extension of the in-transit rule might solve the problem. The hon. member for Winnipeg South, who was a member of the committee, said that it would not. It came out in the short discussion that took place right then, as I read the evidence, that an extension of the in-transit
Railway Act
rule might solve the problem but it would have to be not a slight extension but an extension of considerable degree. It seems to me that would offer a solution of the problem.
I understand that the in-transit rule is applied to the shipment of grain. Grain can start from one point as grain, stop somewhere along the way and be milled into flour, and then be shipped on as flour and the rate paid is the through rate for the total distance. It seems to me that would provide an answer to the problem connected with iron and steel products because that is the feature of most concern to Winnipeg. The board of transport commissioners should find some way to make sure that the total rate for two parts of a distance between two points should never be greater than the through rate between those two points. In other words, if the one and one-third rule is going to place a certain maximum on the rate from Hamilton to Battleford, with which I agree, I submit that the rate on iron and steel products from Hamilton to Battleford, even though they are fabricated along the way at Winnipeg, should not be greater than the through rate which would be possible under the one and one-third rule.
I was interested in the discussion that took place a while ago about the job to be done by the board of transport commissioners in implementing the principles and provisions of this bill. I followed with considerable interest the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Assiniboia, who pointed out that perhaps the major part of this job would be that to be done by the board of transport commissioners after the bill is passed. I hope I am not being unfair to the minister when I say that I think he agrees with the view expressed by the hon. member for Assiniboia. Although he did not want to answer the question as to how long the job would take, it is clear that this matter of implementing these provisions is of concern to the department.
I should like to ask the Minister of Transport if under the bill as it will now go through it is possible for the board of transport commissioners to extend the in-transit principle in such a manner as to solve the kind of problem I have presented to him, which I have taken directly from the Manitoba brief.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
There is a clannishness among the people of the four western provinces which is very worth-while in our Canadian set-up, and I regret that in the argument on this particular section we find ourselves divided.
That division did not start with the members of the house. We all went into the committee believing there was no particular objection to this section, but when we heard

the representations made by the official representatives of the four western provinces we realized that a very difficult question is raised by this particular section. It deals entirely with one group of rates known as transcontinental rates. They are rates which have been established, in effect both east and west, because of the ship competition on the west coast; not only competition from ships carrying goods from eastern Canada through the Panama canal to the Pacific coast, but also ships from abroad. For example there is ship competition from Great Britain with respect to cast iron pipe. Heavy commodities such as cast iron pipe and steel can be carried very easily by ship, and of course can be carried at a low rate.
There can be no doubt that the transcontinental rates are competitive rates. It is true that some of them are very low. For example, the rate on iron pipe is low so the railways can meet the competition of the ships. However, we were told in the committee that there are rates in Ontario and Quebec which are equally low in order to meet truck competition. The point I am trying to make is that these competitive rates to meet carriage by ship are not unduly low. They have been of great benefit to the province of British Columbia because we prefer to get these goods by rail. It is a great deal more advantageous to a businessman to get his supplies by rail because they come a great deal faster than by ship, and there are not the same delays. A ship may have to go to other ports en route, and it is an advantage to be able to get goods by rail.
The transcontinental rates have not only been of benefit to the area or the Pacific coast which includes the cities of Vancouver, Victoria, New Westminster and Prince Rupert, but also to quite a large territory inland from the coast for a distance of approximately one hundred miles. They have been of benefit to the interior of British Columbia because goods transported to the interior get the transcontinental rate plus the rate from Vancouver to the point in question. That is what is known as the back haul, and it is of great benefit to the whole of the interior of British Columbia. It is also of benefit to Alberta cities. Let us take Edmonton, for example. Edmonton gets the benefit of the back haul where there is a transcontinental rate. People there pay the transcontinental rate to Vancouver plus whatever the rate is to carry the goods back from Vancouver to Edmonton. That is cheaper than they would have to pay on a mileage basis coming across

Canada from Ontario or Quebec. I do not believe any hon. member will question that such is the case.
British Columbia is entitled to these transcontinental rates under the laws of Canada as they exist at the present time. That too cannot be denied. On the vast majority of the goods shipped to the west coast we pay the ordinary rates, and we pay the highest rates in Canada. I repeat, we pay the highest rates in Canada on goods coming from eastern Canada with the exception of those few items that are under transcontinental rates. We pay the highest rates also on the great majority of the transcontinental rates. There are only a few of them on which the rate to the coast is lower than the rate to points in Alberta.
Section 331 of the Railway Act contains a code for competitive rates. It sets out what the railways must be able to show if they are to continue a competitive rate. I believe they can bring it into effect without securing the approval of the board but once it has been brought into effect then it can be attacked unless it meets with the requirements set out in section 331. I ask hon. members to look at that section in order to see what those requirements are. Mind you, the competitive rate is lower than the ordinary rates. In the first place it must be shown that competition actually exists. The rate cannot be maintained unless there is competition. Then it must be shown that the rates are compensatory, in other words that the railway is making some money on them. Naturally it will not make as much as it would on the regular rates, but under section 331 the railway cannot carry these goods at a loss under competitive rates. It must also be shown that the rates are not lower than is necessary to meet competition.
These three requirements must be met if the competitive rates are to be kept in effect. Furthermore, such rates are only permissible under our Canadian law where there is competition. They do not apply to intermediate points where there is no competition. Rightly or wrongly it has been the law of Canada that competitive rates would not apply to intermediate points where there was no competition to be met as there is in our case at the coast. There are examples of that right here in Ontario. For example, there is a cheaper rate from Ottawa to Windsor than to London, although the goods go through London on the way. The reason for that is water competition to Windsor and not to London. That evidence was given by the counsel for British Columbia, Mr. Brazier,
Railway Act
and will be found at page 189 of the proceedings of the committee. He pointed out that the rate from Ottawa to Windsor, a distance of 472 miles by water, is 48 cents. The rate to London, a distance of 362 miles, which is not on the water, is 60 cents; that is 12 cents higher than the rate to Windsor. Another example is on the rate from Toronto to Sault Ste. Marie. Reference to that will be found at page 34 of the proceedings, in the evidence of Mr. Evans, vice-president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He pointed out that the Canadian Pacific Railway line from Toronto to Sault Ste. Marie is only 439 miles in length. The Canadian National route from Toronto to Sault Ste. Marie is almost double that length, namely 780 miles; yet the rate over both railways is the same because there is the competition. But the points which are on the way to Sault Ste. Marie on the Canadian National Railways line do not get that reduction. They have to pay the regular mileage.
Another feature about the competitive rates which should be borne in mind is that the railways can increase them or abolish them at will. The board of transport commissioners has no power whatever to prevent the railways increasing a competitive rate, or wiping it out completely. Still another feature is that the areas which qualify for competitive rates are entitled to have the benefit of competition. In other words, on the Pacific coast we are entitled to have both the railway facilities and the ship facilities; just as in Ontario, cities where there is truck competition are entitled to have both the railway service and the truck service. Some hon. members suggested in the committee that because we have the ships therefore we do not need to worry about the rail rates, that it was quite right to take away from us any benefit of bringing freight by rail; but where this competitive situation is definitely established, then the area in question is entitled to have the benefit whatever the competition may be.
So much for the background; let us now come to what section 332B does. It adds to the code set out in section 331 for competitive rates, in the case of transcontinental rates only, a provision that the rates to all intermediate points in the prairie provinces cannot be more than one-third greater than the rate to the coast. There is a ceiling written in on competitive rates for the first time in Canada, and it applies to only one part of the competitive rates, namely those which are transcontinental. Furthermore, section 332B does not say that the one and one-third ceiling shall apply only on the

Railway Act
railway line over which the freight goes- it would not be nearly so objectionable if that were the case-but it defines an area practically from Port Arthur, I think it is, right through to British Columbia. And it says that in that whole area, a thousand miles one way and nearly the same the other, the rate cannot be more than one and one-third the rate to Vancouver.
See what that does. Freight goes to Edmonton, and then it may go 300 or 400 miles north to Waterways or to Grande Prairie in the Peace river country or to Lethbridge down near the United States boundary, and at each of those points the rate must be only one and one-third. That is not the United States system at all. The United States system is that on the line itself the rate must be the same as it is to the coast. They do not take in a huge territory such as has been done in this case.
What is the effect on actual rates? Take canned goods, which are an extreme example because the rate on canned goods is extremely low. It is one of the lowest rates, because ships can put the canned goods in the hold and carry huge quantities of them. I think one ship brought in half a million pounds. I do not remember the figure exactly-we had it in evidence-but it was a huge quantity.
The transcontinental rate to Vancouver and to the coastal territory is $1.57 a hundred pounds. The present rate to Edmonton-if it were on a mileage basis from eastern Canada, it would be $3.23-is only $2.97 because Edmonton gets the benefit of the back haul rate from Vancouver. The rate to Brandon is $2.15. If the one and one-third rule is put in the maximum rate for the whole of the prairie territory will be $2.09, which means that Winnipeg will have to pay just as much to get those canned goods as Waterways will pay away up in northern Alberta. That gives a very clear picture why Manitoba is opposing this section. Incidentally we get a cheap rate on canned goods only in carload lots of 70,000 pounds; in other words a very big car full. On the smaller carload lots of canned goods we pay higher than the rate to Alberta, even on the transcontinental rates. For example, on a carload of 24,000 pounds we pay higher than the rate paid to Alberta.
I hold in my hand a brief submitted by the Vancouver board of trade. They say:
The hoard is much concerned, as also appear to be the railways, that if the commission recommendation, as included in- bill No. 12, is adopted, such losses in revenue would occur to the carriers on traffic to intermediate points that it might be found

necessary by the railways to cancel these transcontinental rates which have been found so beneficial to Vancouver, Victoria, Prince Rupert and other coastal points affected.
An illustration of this rate situation is shown herewith in the transcontinental rate on cast iron pipe from eastern Canada to named Pacific coast points: Group 1, including Vancouver, Victoria, Prince Rupert and New Westminster: $1.12 per 100 pounds.
The minimum car load is 70,000 pounds. There again you have the rate applying only for very large car loads. If you add the 33J per cent to get the rate to intermediate points, it brings it to $1.49 per 100 pounds.
The rate analysis from eastern Canada on this pipe and the estimated loss in revenue to the carriers is indicated to just three stations which are sufficient for the purpose:
They use the round figure of $1.50 instead of $1.49. The present rate to Dawson Creek is $2.61; to Edmonton it is $2.16, and to Saskatoon $1.79. The proposed rate in each case is $1.50. The revenue loss per car load to the carriers amounts to $777 per car load to Dawson Creek, $462 to Edmonton and $203 to Saskatoon. The mileage from Montreal to Dawson Creek is 2,655; to Edmonton, 2,160; to Saskatoon, 1,829. Then the brief goes on:
Should the transcontinental rates be cancelled' the commission plan would' fail as the intermediate points would be assessed present rates and Vancouver and other coast points be penalized. Another important point-the same proposed rate would be authorized to stations with differences in mileage.
I cannot complete my remarks before the dinner recess, but I would point out that the loss in revenue to the railways is not going to come out of the pockets of the railways. It will come out of the shippers or the people in some part of Canada. Do not let any of us believe the railways are going to absorb any of this loss. They do not have to do that.

speechtext:
When the committee rose at 6.15 I had been pointing out that section 332B provides that in the intermediate area the freight rates shall not be higher than

one and one-third of the transcontinental rate, and I went on to explain that this provision applies not only to the line of railway over which the goods move but to the whole territory of the prairie provinces and indeed in Ontario as far east as Fort William and Port Arthur. That provision of course brings into the law a new restriction on competitive rates. A new principle is brought into these rates. It covers a large area running hundreds of miles in both directions.
The result is that on some of the goods the freight rate from eastern Canada will be the same to Winnipeg as it is to Saskatoon, Edmonton and as far away as Waterways. That means a new discrimination in our freight rates, because the people of Winnipeg or the people of Brandon will say, quite rightly:	Why should we have to pay for
this freight the same amount paid by a merchant hundreds of miles away in Edmonton or in Waterways? We are therefore not getting away from discrimination. I think a whole new series of complaints about discrimination in freight rates will be initiated if this section is left without some qualifying provision.
We should also remember that all hope of benefit to Alberta or to western Saskatchewan is based on the railways not increasing these transcontinental rates or wiping them out altogether. Any benefit that is going to come to this intermediate area disappears if the railways see fit to raise the transcontinental rates. The foundation for any relief given by section 332B rests on our transcontinental rates to the Pacific coast.

We should foe delighted to see Alberta get all the benefits possible, but we are afraid that as a result of this plan the transcontinental rates will be wiped out on some goods, or will foe increased. If that happens, Alberta will get no benefit and we will foe penalized. That is the picture.
Then I come to what the railways are likely to do. It must foe remembered that the railways are free to wipe out these transcontinental rates without the board of transport commissioners being able to prevent that action. The vice-president of the. Canadian Pacific Railway gave us figures as to the amount of freight that is involved both in the prairie area and in British Columbia. It is estimated that in the course of the year 1949, under these rates, on goods shipped to British Columbia the C.P.R. earned a total of approximately $1,500,000. On the other hand goods were shipped to the prairie provinces earning in freight the amount of $15,500,000 which might be affected if this new plan is put into effect. That means that on the prairies the amount of freight revenue in danger is ten times that which would be earned in British Columbia by maintaining the transcontinental rates to the coast. As Mr, Evans said, the railways simply will not take that loss. They need not take it because they can increase our transcontinental rates, and it is only human nature to take that step in order to prevent the loss. On that point he is reported at page 43 of the proceedings of the committee as follows:
I submit if it is enacted-

Railway Act
Referring to this section 332B.
-it may result in a breakdown of the entire rate structure, may cause substantial losses in revenue to the railways and may lead to a defeat of its purpose because it will not any longer be possible to maintain the same low basis of transcontinental rates to meet this competition.
That is, to meet the competition by ships. Mr. O'Donnell, counsel for the Canadian National Railways, was examined and at page 202 will be found his answers to questions I asked about getting a guarantee that the transcontinental rate would not be increased. I said:
Would you give us any undertaking that the transcontinental rates would not go up?
I meant if this section becomes law. He replied:

He continued:
I think you have to take it for granted that the railways are out to get all the business they can, even business that they can get on a basis that will make a contribution to their overhead, not necessarily a profit, but a contribution to their overhead; they are going to take it, they will take anything that is going to make money for them.
Now, if the railways decide to make the transcontinental rate high enough so they will not have to lower their rates to intermediate points, and particularly to Edmonton, by reason of this section 332B, the result to British Columbia will be that we will have an increase on approximately 63 per cent of the items which are carried west under this present transcontinental rate. Those figures were furnished to me by the economic expert for the government of British Columbia.
An even more objectionable feature is that in the future the railways will be very reluctant to put in a new transcontinental rate. Here they are faced with a ceiling of one and one-third to apply over the whole area, to practically every station in the prairie provinces, and they will hesitate to put in any new transcontinental rates.
Other areas in Canada are not being treated in that way. They have no such restrictions. Ontario and Quebec receive great benefit from the competitive rates in these two provinces. They receive a great deal more benefit than British Columbia receives from the transcontinental rates. Yet there is no ceiling written on the competitive rates in Ontario and Quebec. If the law of this land is to be that the rates to intermediate points in competitive tariffs must not be more than one and one-third times the rate to the points of competition, then surely it would

only be fair that the rule should apply across the nation and not only to the transcontinental rates.
Some mention was made this afternoon of the origin of this new plan. It came out in evidence before the committee that the provinces had no opportunity to argue it before the royal commission. Apparently the commission got that suggestion from someone-I think from one of their technical men- and it was brought down in the report without the provinces concerned having had the opportunity to point out what the result would be. I think the royal commission did excellent work, but on this one point they should certainly have given the provinces affected an opportunity to come in and be heard, rather than make a recommendation without its having been given full consideration.
I have great sympathy for Alberta. Frankly,
I do not think Saskatchewan is so much concerned. My understanding is that the east half of Saskatchewan will be hurt by the new section, but the west half will be benefited. I repeat, I have great sympathy for Alberta. That province and my own province of British Columbia have more in common than any other two provinces in Canada. I would hope that in the years ahead they will be able to work together very closely. If we do that, then those two provinces will constitute almost an empire.
In my opinion, however, this problem can be met in another way. I believe section 331, dealing with competitive rates, could be amended by putting in that section a provision that where the rate to an intermediate point is over one and one-third the board of transport commissioners will have power to consider whether or not that rate is fair and reasonable. If it were not reasonable, then they would be able to prohibit it, they would be able to cut it down.
There are only a few items causing all this trouble. It is not as though hundreds of freight items were concerned. I believe those causing the serious trouble are the four or five listed in the report of the royal commission. There may be some additional ones, but Mr. O'Donnell said there would not be more than twenty. In order to bring about a fair rate situation with regard to those twenty items, surely the proper way would be to give the board jurisdiction to deal with them, rather than to write an entirely new principle into our law governing competitive rates and restrict that new principle entirely to the transcontinental rates which are beneficial to British Columbia.

Some of these twenty odd items are of great importance in British Columbia. Included, for example, are iron and steel items. If that were not the case I do not suppose there would be much objection to letting it go. But they do enter into our economy to a very large degree, and we have to ask that there be no restriction placed upon the transportation of those goods, such as we believe would follow from section 332B.
That section is out of place in this bill. Here we have a new national freight rates policy. This section does not fit in with that new policy, because it opens the door to new types of discrimination. It is also outside the policy for competitive rates as laid down in the Railway Act. I am afraid it is going to start a lot of fresh trouble out in western Canada, and that is something which certainly should be avoided.
I had intended to quote from some of the briefs filed, but I shall conclude by reading from only one or two of them. The first of these is the brief from the board of trade of Toronto. I would point out that the provincial governments of both Manitoba and British Columbia are opposing this section. Here we have the brief from the board of trade of Toronto, which says:
Section 332B (2a) Maximum tolls to or from intermediate territory.
This board questions the advisability of establishing in statutory form the conditions set forth in this proposed amendment. The railways, in our opinion, should be free to meet any competition actual or potential to Pacific coast points without being obligated to reduce their rates on such traffic to intermediate territory. It is only by their freedom of action to meet such competition that the railways can protect their revenues and at the same time assist Canadian suppliers to meet foreign competition to Pacific coast territory. In its conclusions on the subject of competitive rates generally, the royal commission says on page 86:
"The railways should neither be denied the right to meet competition, nor, when once they have decided to publish competitive tolls in one area, be forced by law to apply these same tolls to other regions where competition between transportation agencies is non-existent."
It is a matter of record that the transcontinental competitive rates have been established only because the railways were faced with competition actual or potential. It is therefore reasonable to conclude that if the railways are to be compelled to extend the benefits of these competitive rates to points where competition is not involved a principle will have been established which it is feared would have a marked influence on the future publication of such rates. Certainly it is difficult to imagine the railways being willing to publish or maintain rates on a competitive basis to the Pacific coast if they were compelled by statute to depress their rates on the same commodities to inland and prairie points where the competition did not exist. In such a situation, it is possible that the railways may have to reconsider their position respecting these rates and in that event it is conceivable that they may be forced to cancel the transcontinental rates and probably be compelled also to review the existing
Railway Act
system of publishing competitive rates in the light of the possible general effects such legislation may have on these rates.
I think that sums up the situation very neatly. I would hope that the minister would give the section further consideration and possibly agree to an amendment which would give the board power to review any of these rates which are over one and one-third and cut them down to that figure if they are found to be unreasonable.
There are nearly two million people in British Columbia and Manitoba, and about the same number in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and I doubt the wisdom of adopting a policy on which there is such a wide difference of opinion. It cannot be good legislation when there are such large blocks of people who will be dissatisfied. For that reason alone I submit that the government is unwise to force through section 33 2B in the form in which it is now found in the bill.

speechtext: The point is this. Let me tell my hon. friend that if we did not have this bill all the things that Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have been complaining about over the years would not be remedied. All the provinces would go back before the board of transport commissioners under the circumstances as they were before, and the board would have its hands tied by judicial judgments handed down over the years. There would be no remedy at all for the present position. For the last forty-seven years the board of transport commissioners has been trying to remedy this position and could not do so because it did not have the power. We in this parliament decided that we would have a royal commission to investigate their complaints. After all, we must be logical. Did we not say to the provinces in effect-and when I say "we" I mean the government- all right; you want a royal commission, but you will have to take the bitter with the sweet. I am not admitting there is anything bitter in this bill. I do not think there is. With all due respect to my hon. friend-

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Surely it was never the position that the provinces had to take whatever the royal commission chose to bring in without any opportunity to protest and ask for something else. That is making the royal commission almost godlike. Nobody thought they were that.

No. I agree with my hon. friend that nobody thought they were that, but I think it might be interesting if I were to read to the house something that is contained in the brief of the premiers of the provinces to the government, and this is an entirely different citation from the one I put on the record before. I place this one on the record because it has particular reference to the problem under discussion now. Here is what the brief said at one point:
In our opinion the only satisfactory way in which this problem can be met is by the appointment of a royal commission under the public inquiries act. The differences between the views of the seven provinces and the view of the federal government in this matter are not fundamental differences in any matter of principle.
The dominion government feels that there should be a further inquiry into this matter. The seven provinces are unanimously of the same mind. The only question between us is as to the body which should conduct the inquiry and we feel that a royal commission can perform this duty with greater satisfaction than can the board of railway commissioners. We give the following reasons in support of our view:
(a) With wide powers of reference enabling it to inquire into all railway problems of the country

Railway Act
as they exist in either a geographic or an economic sense with full power to recommend any amendment to existing legislation or as to the constitution, powers and duties of the regulatory body, it can do much to promote a greater sense of national and regional security in the dominion. We feel an opportunity should be given to the provinces to make recommendations with regard to the terms of reference of the royal commission.
(b) If the commission is composed of men of ability with an urge to inquiry constructively for solutions to problems now vexatious and pressing, such a commission could without spending too much time in hearing evidence arrive at conclusions calculated to advance the general welfare.
And we proceeded-

speechtext: Surely the minister is not suggesting that the provinces bound themselves by that request to accept whatever recommendations the commission saw fit to bring down.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
No, I am not arguing that, but my hon. friend will see in a moment what I am coming to. This brief was read by one of the premiers, and at the end of the brief is to be found this addendum:
The submission which I make has the unanimous assent and approval of the premiers of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia. The premier of British Columbia is unable to be here today because of the demands of his own legislative session; but he was with us all day Saturday, on which day the proposals that I have outlined were discussed and agreed to by the seven premiers. I am authorized by Premier Johnson of British Columbia to say that, joining with the other provinces in the proposals now submitted, the premier of the province of British Columbia thinks it proper that it be made known to the dominion cabinet that the province of British Columbia had, prior to the judgment of the board, taken appropriate steps toward the filing of applications with the board of transport commissioners for the approval of the mountain differential, and intends to proceed thereon with all due diligence.
The province of British Columbia did proceed with the application to the board for the removal of the mountain differential, and the board granted the application. My hon. friend says: "Surely you are not arguing that the provinces are bound by these recommendations." I am not arguing that, but what I am arguing is that the provinces wanted the royal commission and in effect said: "There is no difference of opinion between us in principle. The only difference of opinion is that you want an investigation under P.C. 1487; we want a royal commission. Give us a royal commission and also let us assist you on the terms of reference." We have done that. Could we go any further than we have gone? Having read the report, having studied the report, having examined the conclusions, we adopted them. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was also of the view that these recommendations were good. He was not only of the view that they were good-and now I refer to section 332B

-but that they should be brought down and implemented at the earliest opportunity. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra made a lengthy speech when I dealt with the recommendations on the report of the royal commission in the house-and a very good speech it was-which indicated that he had studied the report of the royal commission very carefully. He dealt with many of the recommendations therein contained, and he dealt in an especial manner with section 332B. I am sure he will not object if I read to the committee what he said then. This was his statement on April 5, 1951.' It can be found at page 1649 of Hansard:
Another subject which Is also of great importance and which likewise calls for an amendment to the Railway Act is that of transcontinental rates. They are dealt with at page 96 of the report, and I refer particularly to page 101 where it is stated;
"The Railway Act should be amended to provide that when the competitive transcontinental tariffs are published by the railways, such tariffs shall contain a provision that the rates to or from intermediate territory shall not exceed the transcontinental rates by more than one-third."
As I understand it, the meaning of that recommendation is this. There are certain special transcontinental rates, for example, from Toronto and Montreal to Vancouver. They are only in effect because there is competition by sea and we benefit by those rates on the west coast. I presume there is also a similar benefit from transcontinental rates on the east coast. But the Canadians who live in the interior part of the country-for example, in interior British Columbia, in Alberta and, I suppose, in Saskatchewan as well-do not get any benefits from those transcontinental rates. They must pay a much higher rate. The commission has recommended that the higher rate that they pay in the interior portions of the country shall not be more than one-third higher than the transcontinental rates. I believe that that provision, if it became law, would be of great benefit to those Canadians who are not privileged to live at the seashore. I hope that the government will bring in an amendment to the Railway Act at this session to make that change possible as well.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I am suggesting that the members of the royal commission were men qualified to deal with this problem. opportunity of discussing this recommendation. But did the provinces have any opportunity of discussing the other recommendations contained in this report? The report goes on to say that no great hardship, if any at all, will ensue to the province of British Columbia. I could quote that chapter at length, but I shall not do that. If hon. members will read the conclusions at the bottom of page 99 of the royal commission report, together with the five or six paragraphs to be found on page 100, they will find what the commission recommended in so far as the one and one-third rule is concerned.
Then my hon. friends suggest we should amend section 331 in order to give the board authority to deal with the one and one-third rule. But that would not meet the position in Alberta. Alberta is faced with section 314, subsection 5, of the Railway Act which, because of the competitive transcontinental rate to the coast, puts that province in an unfair discriminatory position. The way to remedy that is not by amending section 331, but by a new section in the bill. If I were to accept the suggestion made by the hon. member it would interfere with the right of the railways to establish competitive rates. After all, the competitive rate is one which the railways file with the board of transport commissioners. The answer to that, Mr. Chairman, is that the commission dealt with in-transit or stop-off rates in a special chapter, and came to the conclusion that it would not begin to answer the problems of Alberta and Saskatchewan. They recommended against it. If my hon. friend will look at page 113 of the commission's report, he will find a chapter or a section of a chapter dealing with stop-off privileges. The conclusion reached by the royal commission is as follows:
The reasons for the establishment of stop-off (or in-transit) privileges are stated above, and it must be borne in mind that these privileges are concessions made by the railways.
To carry out the proposal suggested by Alberta would lead to the introduction of claims for further stop-off privileges on the grounds of analogy to existing cases and in turn to reductions of revenue to the railways. It is presumed that the railways are competent to determine what stop-off privileges are in their interests and it would be dangerous to permit the board to compel them to act against their interests and to commit them to indefinite losses.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Will the minister explain the amendment to section 18, and tell us just how this section will be applied?

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Section 18 is the subsidy section having to do with the payment of $7 million to both railways. By virtue of subsection 1 (a) the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is to receive the full annual cost of maintaining 552 miles of trackage, subject to subsection 4, if the total cost for both railways exceeds $7 million. By virtue of subsection 1 (b) the Canadian National Railway is to receive the full annual cost of maintaining 552 miles of trackage out of the total trackage involved of 985 miles, subject also to the provisions of subsection 4. By virtue of subsection 2 the board of transport commissioners is to determine what actual trackage is to be used, which would mean that it would fix the actual trackage to be included, such as the main track, the passing track, the siding, the yards and the like. The board is also to determine, by virtue of this section the annual cost to each for the trackage so determined and for inclusion in the scope of the payment.
These payments should be for the purpose of reducing to that extent the freight rates applying between eastern and western Canada, and the amendment which has been added indicates how the board is to proceed. The total amount payable shall be applied to a reduction of the relative level of rates applying on freight traffic moving 'in both directions between points in eastern Canada and points in western Canada over the trackage to which the payment relates, in such manner as the board may allow or direct. In effect the board of transport commissioners, which is the body dealing with these rates, will determine the coverage as to tracks applying to both railways, and will also determine the manner in which this $7 million shall be apportioned.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTING CERTAIN RECOMMENDATIONS OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
The $7 million provision in this section should result in some benefits to the people of the prairies and to the long haul shippers. It has been stated over and over again that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have certain natural advantages in the way of truck and water competition which result in low competitive rates for the people in this area:	The long haul shipper, even
though the rates may be equalized, needs something more; and that something more, as suggested by the royal commission, is this $7 million to pay the cost of maintenance of the trackage over the railway bridge between east and west.
Railway Act
We should bear in mind first of all the fact that this amount is only $7 million; and unless the $7 million is guarded carefully this provision may not result-if certain other things are done-in any benefit whatsoever to western Canada. Up until now freight rates have been set on the basis of using the financial position of the Canadian Pacific Railway as a yardstick. One of the important items in that C.P.R. yardstick was that freight rates should be of such an order as to provide the C.P.R. with a surplus of $15 million. I note that at the present time there is a move on foot by the C.P.R. to get the $15 million surplus in the C.P.R. formula increased to a figure of between $27 million and $29 million. If the C.P.R. can get the formula changed so that in future freight rates are set so as to give it a surplus of $29 million instead of a surplus of $15 million, there will have to be an increase in freight rates to the extent of $52 million; and on the basis of estimates made in the past the total cost of changing the C.P.R. surplus from $15 million to $29 million would amount to some $30 million for freight users in western Canada.
All I am saying is this. If, a few days after we are given the $7 million to maintain the trackage over that bridge, we are called upon to pay another $30 million in freight rates in order to provide more money to the C.P.R., it would have been better for the government to keep the $7 million and not spend it, and not to have made this provision in the bill, if at the same time the government would prevent this proposed change in the C.P.R. formula. I want the $7 million, but I want it to be effective in bringing down the rates for the freight users in western Canada. It will not be effective if, after the government provides the $7 million, a change is granted by the board of transport commissioners in the C.P.R. formula on which freight rates are based, in order to provide the C.P.R. with more money at a cost of $30 million to the freight users in western Canada.
We want equalized freight rates; but the advantages of equalized freight rates will be small indeed if they are increased by the suggested new formula. I do not know whether the minister is prepared to comment on the argument I have made. But I can say to him that I hope, I trust, the government will see to it that the Canadian Pacific formula is not changed, because that would result in taking away all the benefits of the $7 million, and impose an additional burden on western Canada.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES  ADDITION OF PROTOCOL DEALING WITH EXCHANGE OF RATIFICATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 28, to amend an act to amend the Canada-United States of America Tax Convention Act, 1943, and the Canada-United States of America Tax Convention Act, 1944.
He said: Parliament recently approved the supplementary income tax convention with the United States of America which amended the income tax convention which had existed since March 4, 1942. The supplementary convention was approved by chapter 27 of the statutes of 1950. The protocol which has now been added to the supplementary convention accepts on the part of the government of Canada the reservation which was made by the government of the United States, on the advice of its Senate, to the effect that paragraph 2 of article VII of the original convention as amended by article I (d) of the supplementary convention should be deleted. Article VII reads:
1.	A resident of Canada shall be exempt from United States income tax upon compensation for labour or personal services performed within the United States of America if he conforms to either of the following conditions:
(a) He is temporarily present within the United States of America for a period or periods not exceeding a total of one hundred and eighty-three days during the taxable year and such compensation
(A)	is received for labour or personal services performed as an employee of, or under contract with, a resident corporation or other entity of Canada and
(B)	does not exceed $5,000 in the aggregate during such taxable year; or (b) he is temporarily present in the United States of America for a period or periods not exceeding a total of ninety days during the taxable year and the compensation received for such services does not exceed $1,500 in the aggregate during such taxable year.
2.	The provisions of paragraph 1 (a) of this article shall have no application to ihe professional earnings of such individuals as actors, artists, musicians and professional athletes.

146$
Canada-U.S.A. Tax Convention Acts
The one hundred and eighty-three days referred to do not have to be consecutive. In its reservation to the ratification of the convention the government of the United States did not accept the provision which restricted the article dealing with compensation for personal services in the case of actors, artists, musicians and athletes. That is one point being dealt with in this amendment.
Article VII, which I have just quoted, provided that a resident of Canada would be exempt from United States tax upon compensation for personal or professional services performed within the United States if he was present therein for less than one hundred and eighty-three days during the year and met certain conditions as to the residence of his employer or the amount received for his personal services, which I have indicated would be less than $5,000.
An exemption with respect to the application of this provision was made with respect to the professional earnings of such individuals as actors, artists, musicians and professional athletes. The United States senate committee which examined the convention considered that this restriction embodied a discriminatory principle which the committee could not accept. This bill will confirm the government of Canada's acceptance of that same reservation and will remove the restriction relating to actors, artists, musicians and athletes. The result will be that actors, artists, musicians and athletes from one country receiving remuneration for services performed in the other country will be treated for income tax purposes in the same way as commercial travellers, professional men, and others. The provisions are reciprocal and apply to Canadians who receive remuneration for services performed in the United States and to United States residents who receive remuneration for services performed in Canada. If you will look at the bill you will see that the only words added to section 1 are "and protocol". The section will read:
The convention and protocol entered into between Canada and the United States of America, set out in schedule A-
That is the schedule at the back of the bill.
-is approved and declared to have the force of law in Canada, and shall be deemed to be included in and to form part of the convention and protocol set out in the schedule to the Canada-United States of America Tax Convention Act, 1943.
